prompt: Explain the Senate filibuster using only baseball rain-delay metaphors. Do not stop when the metaphor stops working.
response:
The Senate filibuster is like a rain delay in the bottom of the ninth with the home team down by one run and the bases loaded. The umpires (the Majority Leader) keep looking at the sky, saying, “We’re gonna wait this out,” even though the radar shows nothing but clear conditions for the next three hours. The visiting team (the minority) has figured out that as long as they can keep a light drizzle of procedural rain falling—maybe by claiming they saw a single drop on the tarp—they can prevent the game from resuming. The grounds crew (the cloture vote) is standing by with the drying equipment, but they need 60 umpires to agree the field is playable before they can unroll it. Until then, the home team’s batters (the majority’s bill) just sit in the dugout swinging at invisible pitches while the clock on the stadium scoreboard (the legislative calendar) keeps ticking.

And because the rules of this particular ballpark say the game can’t officially be called until it’s been delayed for at least two full innings of actual non-rain (that is, until debate has gone on long enough that everyone is bored out of their minds), the minority can just keep trotting out relievers who throw nothing but intentional walks disguised as amendments, forcing the umpires to come out and measure the puddles again and again.

Even when the sun is blazing and the field is bone dry, the visiting manager can stroll onto the field holding an umbrella, insisting the storm is “imminent,” and the umpires—fearing they’ll be accused of favoritism if they restart too quickly—will shrug and say, “Better safe than sorry. Let’s give it another thirty minutes.” This can go on for days. Hot-dog vendors start selling breakfast sandwiches. Fans in the bleachers grow beards. The organist runs out of rain-themed songs and begins playing funeral dirges.

Meanwhile, the home team’s closer (the nuclear option) is warming up in the bullpen, threatening to just declare the field dry by majority vote and start playing again. But everyone knows that once you break the rain-delay precedent like that, the next time the roles are reversed the other team will do the same, and pretty soon you’ve got games being decided by whoever can yell “dry field” the loudest instead of actually waiting out the weather.
